speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That on Wednesday, the 21st of May instant, and subsequent Wednesdays to the end of the session, government notices of motion and government orders shall have precedence over all 'business except questions by members and notices of motions for the production of papers.

Business of the House
* Mr. HARRY LEADER (Portage la Prairie): I beg humbly to protest against this resolution. It will have the effect of taking away private members' day thereby preventing hon. members from bringing resolutions before the House. I know the Prime Minister will say that we have all had opportunity to present our resolutions. That is true. In regard to the resolution that stands on the order paper in my name, I may say that I had three opportunities to bring it forward: one on a Monday night at a quarter to eleven; another on a Thursday night at a quarter to ten; and I think another on a Wednesday night at twenty minutes to six. But had I gone on with my resolution on any of those occasions I should perhaps only have had the opportunity of speaking myself; then the debate would have been adjourned and the motion would not have been voted upon. Now, this happened last year and I did not intend that the same thing should occur this year. I thought I had my resolution in in lots of time, but evidently there was so much other work ahead that it was not reached. However, I should like to take this opportunity of protesting against taking Wednesday as proposed. I might mention that a number of hon. gentlemen when speaking during the budget debate referred to the fact that if we desired to practise economy we should start here and set an example to the country by agreeing to a reduction in our sessional indemnity.
Order. Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion?

Mr. Speaker I also wish to protest not so much perhaps at the actual motion as at the situation which results from the practice of late years of filling up the order paper with motions. sometimes before the House meets at all. For instance when we came down here first this session there were already three or four pages of notices of motion. Some of them were-I do not think I would be over harsh in saying this-of an absolutely unnecessary kind, resolutions of an abstract character -one for example dealing with what Britain should do about the Ruhr. What on earth have we here got to do with the Ruhr? I should like to know what practical end can be achieved by discussing abstract questions of that sort. There are many more such resolutions; I could point out a dozen that are equally useless as far as the actual operation of lawmaking here is concerned. What I wanted to say is this:	These motions are
put on the order paper and frequently not taken up when called. As the Prime Min-
141i
ister said on a previous occasion some of them have been called six times and still they maintain their place on the order paper. Two resolutions stand on the order paper in my name. They are unimportant, I will admit. One was the notice of a bill, and the other was the notice of a resolution that I wanted to discuss. Both however would be of some practical advantage-at least I should hope so-as regards the interests of Canada. I put these resolutions on the order paper within a month after the House met, but of course there were a great number of motions ahead of them. They never were called except on one occasion when a number of the members were going to Halifax. I stayed away from that trip on purpose because I thought my motion would come up. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, it came up on the occasion in question at three minutes to six and by speaking to the motion I obtained the placing of it on the order paper amongst public bills and orders instead of it remaining amongst motions. Now, private members' day has been taken from us and the resolution will not come up again. If I am not very much mistaken there have been fewer days devoted to the motions of private members this session than in any other session for a long number of years past-at least for some ten or twelve years. I quite admit that a remedy is needed but I do not think it is the remedy such as suggested by the motion before the House. What I would suggest is this: That the House or the government should consider amending the rules in the following manner: First, that when these motions are called and not gone on with, unless in case of the sickness of the hon. member in whose name they stand, they shall be dropped and have to be placed at the bottom of the order paper again. That -would give hon. members who have something that they really desire to bring before the House a chance to be heard. The second amendment I would suggest is, instead of going along two or three months, and then arbitrarily saying, "We cannot have any more private members' days," that after an agreed on date-say a couple of months after the opening of the House-no more new motions would be accepted; so that no one could put any fresh notice on the order paper, but that members who had notices then on the order paper which had not been called should be given an opportunity to be heard. So far as I am concerned, I am quite willing to forego the opportunity of talking on the matter I am interested in, in order to choke off a lot of these vague abstract resolutions that are before us. But some day, when the government or the opposition, as the case might
Business oj the House

be, are desperately in need of an opportunity to move some particular motion, it could be easily blocked by the opposition or the government putting a lot of abstract motions on the order paper, and then when they were forced to, taking up one order or the other until the time lapsed. But any bona fide motion put on the order paper within two months-or one month, if you like-of the opening of the House would be heard. The other sugestion of dropping those motions that were not called would facilitate, and perhaps put an end to what I really think is'an abuse of the original intention of the rules.

When the
matter of taking Mondays came up some weeks ago I made a protest against the motion which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) brought in. However, my protest was unavailing. I have taken the trouble to look into the record of this House for the last thirty years in respect to private members' day, and I must say that the information which I secured in that investigation certainly is not creditable to the present government, or the present parliament, or the present procedure. I am not going to weary the House by giving them the details at the present time, I am simply going to say that in the old days there was practically always plenty of time taken to reasonably clear the order paper of these private members' resolutions. Twenty years ago Thursdays were taken first, Wednesdays were taken next, and Monday was left a complete day when a vote might be had-Monday was left until the last. This year, for the first time, the procedure has been reversed and Monday has been taken first, and that is the only day when a vote can be secured. I may say the record of this House is indeed worse than the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has intimated. So far as Mondays, which are the only days that really concern us, are concerned, we have had nineteen days between the time that the debate on the Address was concluded, and the date that Monday was taken, and there were twenty-nine private members' motions left on the order paper unconsidered. Since the time I made this record I think there has been an addition of several to the list. No other year in the last thirty approaches anywhere near that record. There were one or two years during the war when there were not very many resolutions on the orders, and when-probably for special reasons-the number of days allowed for private members was smaller than it was, say about three or four years ago. This matter is not concluded; it will come up again; and I want to protest that the rules of the House 
in this respect ought to be amended. I am not prepared to endorse the suggestions already made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), but I do think this is a matter of great importance, because, as I said before, private members are figuring and will figure in the future more prominently in the business of the House than under the two party system, and we must have some extension or rearrangement. I was going to suggest, without debating the matter at any great length- I do not want to go into any further argument-that we ought to have a full day, say Monday, for practically the entire session, and let the government have Wednesdays, when they can take up estimates, or something of that nature without any trouble at all. They are now of practically no use for private members' resolutions, as they can be talked out. The government and the members know this, and why do they not look at it in a sensible way, and give some consideration to private members? I am not going to do anj'thing further at the present time, but I want to warn the government that they have not heard the last of the matter.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. JAMES MURDOCK (Minister of Labour) moved that the House go into Committee of the Whole on Monday next to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to confirm a certain Convention relating to the employment of children at sea, adopted at Genoa on the 9th day of July, 1920, by a general Conference of the International Labour Organization of the League of Nations; and to provide that no child under the age of fourteen years shall be employed on any ship except as permitted under such convention; that a list of persons under sixteen years of age so employed, or a register thereof, shall be kept; that penalties be imposed for violation of the proposed legislation; and that the Act shall not apply where all the crew are members of the same family, or the child was lawfully employed at the commencement of the Act.
He said: His Excellency the Governor General, having be.en made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the favourable consideration of the House.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: RESIGNATION OF MR. WALTER G. MITCHELL
speechtext: I saw a message to the press from Mr. Mitchell, in which he mentioned that the communication that he had sent to me was a private one, and I think it probably should be for' him to make his own explanation. I do not know that I am expected to.

maintopic: RESIGNATION OF MR. WALTER G. MITCHELL
speechtext: Did the Prime Minister say that according to the press despatch, Mr. Mitchell said that the communication to the Prime Minister was private?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: RESIGNATION OF MR. WALTER G. MITCHELL
speechtext:
I saw a communication to a member of the press from Mr. Mitchell, from New York, in which communication he said that he had given his reasons to me in a private letter. The mention of the letter as being private causes me at this moment to say that it is for Mr. Mitchell himself to make known its contents to the public should he so desire.
Supply-Agriculture

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Marcil (Bonaventure) in the chair:
Agriculture-health of animals (administration and enforcement of Animal Contagious Diseases Act and Meat and Canned Foods Act), $2,000,000.

Will the minister kindly
give to the committee some particulars with regard to the dismissal of the late Veterinary Director General?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: The st.ory is a fairly long one and I do not _want to make it any longer than I can help, but that depends upon how much information my hon. friend requires. The recent Veterinary Director General placed upon file with my department correspondence that he had with an appointee at Washington holding the same position there as he did here, complaining of the Veterinary department in connection with the administration of this particular appropriation being administered politically. I can read the parts of the letter that I have reference to, if the committee so desires; but it is of such an extraordinary nature from my standpoint that I asked Dr. Torrance for an explanation of it, why he sent to an officer holding a similar position to his in Washington a letter of this nature and also where the political interference was on the part of mysel'f or the government in the administration of the department, especially in connection with the embargo on our cattle going to Great Britain and the quarantine provisions in relation thereto. He stated that the interference complained of referred, not to the Canadian government, but to the British government. That seemed so absurd that it was no excuse, so I told him I thought the time had arrived when we should dissolve partnership. We discussed the matter in a business way and he thought he would retire' under the provisions of the Calder Act. This was quite agreeable to me. I am willing to read the letter to the committee or to place it on file.
When the minister suggested the dissolution, did he suggest that he himself be the party to leave instead of the official?

I had no idea of
that and I have no idea yet. Dr. Torrance has a position in another part of this province.
Does the minister suggest that he could not get one?

No. I am very
glad that he did get one.

Any suggestion that the
minister himself could not get a position, so that that was the better way out of the matter?

No. If my hon.
friend wants a scrap, I am ready for him. We have done a good day's work already, and if he wants to start right now, I am willing to start. I am not particular whether I get this vote through to-day or not, if that is the humour my right hon. friend is in. I am trying to give the limited amount of information out of consideration of Dr. Torrance. We got on very nicely together; but a document of this nature, even though it is a private document, placed upon file in the office of a foreign government, could not be tolerated. That is all there is to the matter.
Was the letter a personal communication to the chief of the Bureau at Washington?
Yes.
WTil! the minister read it?
It was a personal letter written by Dr. Torrance to Dr. Mohler, but the whole staff was aware of the fact that it had been sent.
How did the minister get possession of it?
It was sent to my office by Dr. Torrance.
Had a copy been kept of it?	[DOT]
It was sent to my office, that is all I know.
Then I take it that the letter would be in the nature of a public communication.
Well, so far as Dr. Mohler was concerned it was private; it was marked " confidential."

But who gave
this confidential communication to the minister?
Dr. Torrance.
Did the minister ask Dr. Torrance for it?
No.
I should think it would be a pretty good letter. Perhaps the minister would have no objection to reading it.
Dr. Torrance showed it to me after he had sent it.

What is the nature of the letter?

Supply-A griculture

I think I had better read the whole of it. As I have said, it is marked confidential and is dated October 28, 1922. It reads:
Dr. J. R. Mohler,
Chief, Bureau of Animal Industry,
Washington, D.C.
Dear Mr. Mohler :
You are no doubt familiar with the fact that the negotiations for the removal of the British embargo against Canadian cattle have reached the point where a discussion of details is taking place. The Canadian delegates in England are discussing these questions with the British government and information has reached me that it is quite probable we may. be asked to modify the Canadian Quarantine Regulations as regards imports of cattle from Great Britain.
You might have noticed that when the Canadian case was being argued before the British Commission it was suggested that if Great Britain removed the embargo against Canadian cattle and allowed them to enter Great Britain freely, that Canada should reciprocate by permitting British cattle to enter Canada under similar conditions. Dr. Tolmie, who was representing Canada at that time, stated that if health conditions in Great Britain, with regard to live stock, were as satisfactory as they are in Canada, such a proposition might meet with favourable consideration, but that he did not consider the cases were parallel, and pointed out the frequent outbreaks of foot and mouth disease from which Great Britain had suffered in recent years.
It is quite possible, however, that a suggestion may be made that we should modify our quarantine so as to reduce the time of detention, and it is with regard to this possible demand that I would like to have confidentially your opinion as it affects the relations between the Bureau and the Health of Animals Branch. We have always felt that we were under agreement not to alter our quarantine regulations without previously notifying you of our intention, and we have received from you the same consideration.
I am strongly of the opinion that quarantine regulations should be based upon scientific knowledge of the diseases against which we desire protection, of the conditions surrounding the traffic in animals, the freedom from disease of the country from which the cattle are exported, and the time occupied in ocean travel. If political considerations are to be introduced into the consideration of the question of quarantine it places the scientific advisers of the respective governments in a very anomalous position, and I feel that where we have to undertake the responsibility of carrying out any regulations that are made we should also have a decided influence in the planning of these regulations.
Should political pressure force me to accept a shortened period of quarantine for imports from the British Isles I have been wondering what would be the attitude of your Bureau in regard to the matter. I have, therefore, thought it well to consult you privately before the matter has reached a decision, and I would appreciate anything you may say and treat it as confidential if you desire me to do so. You may, therefore, feel quite at liberty to tell me frankly what your opinion of the situation is, and what you think would be the result upon our mutual relations regarding the traffic in cattle across our border should any such action as that suggested be taken.
With kind regards, and thanking you in anticipation of your prompt reply, I am,
Yours sincerely,
F. Torrance.
This letter will probably appear unintelligible to the committee unless hon. members know certain facts. Dr. Torrance, naturally enough, wanted to be one of the delegates who should go overseas. Two gentlemen went over, Dr. Grisdale and Mr. Duncan Marshall, and they were accompanied by two ministers. They went for the purposes of conference and I considered that such a representation of the department was ample. Dr. Torrance made it known quite candidly to me that he thought he should be one of those to go overseas and apparently-I suppose quite naturally-he was disappointed at not having been permitted to go. I ex- plained to him that in my opinion two delegates in addition to the two ministers were quite sufficient for the purposes we had in mind. I drew his attention to the following paragraph in the letter as well as to the two preceding it:
Should political pressure force me to accept a shortened period of quarantine for imports from the British Isles I have been wondering what would be the attitude of your Bureau in regard to the matter.
I asked Dr. Torrance to explain to what this paragraph had reference and he said that it related to political interference on the part of the British government. I replied that this was nonsense inasmuch as we had never heard for many years of any such interference. I was not aware of anything of the kind nor did anyone else know anything about it and I intimated that in my judgment there was no justification for the writing of such a document.
Will the minister read the reply to that letter?

The reply is not
on the file but the substance of it was that the desire was to carry out the old arrangements with regard to quarantine. '

The minister says that
this letter was written on October 28, 1922. It seems to me that it took rather a long time for the gentleman to hand it over to him. How does it come that so long a time elapsed before the minister got hold of the letter?
Before taking action I was anxious to see whether this was typical of the manner in which Dr. Torrance had administered the department or whether it was merely an isolated case.
The question is when did the minister get the letter?

I do not recall
when I got it.
Mr. CIIAPIjlN:	Was it long ago or
recently?

I received the letter shortly after it was written.
And apparently the minister waited some time before taking action.
Yes I was waiting for some corroborative evidence that would either confirm or rebut the suggestion that this was the manner in w'hich, on the whole, Dr. Torrance administered the department.

And what is the nature
of the "corroborative evidence" which the minister received?

I will give that,
too.
Yes, come along with it.

In justice to Dr.
Torrance I want to say that such evidence as existed tending to show dereliction of duty on his part in other respects, was not, I thought, in itself sufficient to warrant dismissal, or, to put it in a nicer way, to warrant the severance of our relations.
Or, the dissolving of the partnership. That was the first phrase used and it is so good that I do not like to see it dropped.

Well, that would
be a satisfactory term. I say that none of the reasons that have been enumerated on these pages would be sufficient in themselves, because a great many of them are incapable of proof. But, taking them in conjunction with this correspondence, I felt that there was ample warranty for the action I took in regard to Dr. Torrance.

Perhaps I am a little
dense, but I do not quite understand yet, having- heard the letter read, wherein the offence consists; I do not see the crime in it. Perhaps the minister would be good enough to explain to us, who are not so familiar with agricultural conditions, just what is wrong about the letter.

He is suggesting
that the whole question of embargo and quarantine is being administered politically.
Oh, no, not at all.
Yes.
Where does he say that?

All right, we will
read it over again. Dr. Torrance writes:
I am strongly of the opinion that quarantine regulations should be based upon scientific knowledge of the diseases against which we desire protection of the conditions surrounding traffic in animals, the freedom

from disease of the country from which the cattle are exported, and the time occupied in ocean travel.
If political considerations are to be introduced into the consideration of the question of quarantine it places the scientific advisers of the respective governments in a very anomalous position and I feel that where we have to undertake the responsibility of carrying out any regulations that are made we should also have a decided influence in the planning of these regulations.
What he had in mind there was that he should not only have framed the regulations but should have gone over to Great Britain and negotiated any change therein. I know that, for he had a conversation with me regarding it.
What was the conversation?
That he should go to Great Britain as one of the representatives.

Is the fact that he
wanted to go to Great Britain as one of our representatives, apparently instead of Mr. Duncan Marshall, part of the corroborative evidence?
.Mr. MOTHERWELL: No. If I had not known what was in his mind I would have been more astounded by the nature of this letter. But I do know that he wanted to go.

What is wrong with
that?

I do not know
whether what he had in mind as "political interference" was the appointment of my deputy or of Mr. Duncan Marshall.

He does not
say it was either.

The whole thing
was so astounding that when I asked him candidly what he meant, he said that he meant interference by the British government. I pointed out that that could not be so, and he did not say any more.

I think the committee
ought to get a clear perspective of this incident,-I call it an incident, but it is a great deal more when it affects an individual of the standing of Dr. Torrance. We have here one of the most flagrant violations of the statutes of Canada, indeed, a defiance of those statutes, that perhaps could be imagined. In 1920 this parliament passed the Civil Service Act. We all know perfectly well that the task of the Civil Service Commission was a tremendous one and could not result in complete harmony and success in the course of a few years. We also realize that the Civil Service Commission has not in

Supply-Agriculture
all its activities given complete satisfaction to everybody. But the principle and the idea behind the legislation has appealed to the people and has been accepted by the Civil Service generally as a very welcome protection against unreasonable interference. Here was a civil servant of high standing whom the minister dismissed at a moment's notice, as I will show in a moment. He brings to the House
a letter_a copy of which I have under my
hand and which I shall analyze, perhaps a little more fully and a little more fairly than the minister has yet done-and he admits that that letter alone is not sufficient justification for his action in dismissing the Doctor. Then he holds in his hand what he terms "corroborative evidence." And what does he say about that corroborative evidence? Without presenting it he says: Well, I admit it is not very significant and the offence is not serious.

I will read it all
if you wish.

And he says that it could not be proved. Furthermore, as the final and deciding factor in the case, he states that he knew Dr. Torrance had some idea in the back of his mind. That is a pretty flimsy ground upon which to dismiss a civil servant of the standing of Dr. Torrance. Now, let us examine the letter. I want the committee to bear in mind that the charge against Dr. Torrance was that he had declared there was political pressure being brought to bear upon him. That is the charge of the minister. Let ns see upon what it is based. The letter, written by Dr. Torrance, head of the Health of Animals branch, is addressed to Dr. J. R. Mohler, chief of the Bureau of Animals Industry in Washington. The letter is marked *"confidential"; it was confidential between these two gentlemen. Now let us get the perspective. Dr. Torrance and Dr. Mohler administer the Health of Animals in their respective countries. In order that the quarantine regulations of Canada and the United States, regulations which are always irritating in a measure to these who are subject to them, should be carried out with as little irritation to the public as possible, these two chief officials of their respective governments were in constant touch and working in substantial harmony. Let me give an illustration to show there was nothing sinister in Dr. Torrance's action. Take the inmigration authorities-and my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) who handles that branch is now in his seat and will bear me out-supposing the immigration
authorities of Canada and the United States did not work in harmony in many respects, would there not be tremendous irritation to the public? My hon. friend will agree with that. It is one" of those little courtesies between officials of two governments which is necessary if friendly relations are to continue.
I am not going to read the whole letter because it is already on Hansard. The first portion the minister will not himself complain of in the slightest degree; it is a reference to the foot and mouth disease. At this time negotiations were on foot with Great Britain. Great Britain was demanding that her animals should have access to our market with a minimum of quarantine and a lowering of the standard of the regulations which at that time obtained. But it must be borne in mind that even in that very year there were twenty-two cases of foot and mouth disease in Great Britain. To show that Dr. Torrance's and Dr. Mohler's apprehensions were well founded, all I have to do is to remind the committee that since that time, animals to the value of millions of pounds sterling have been destroyed in Great Britain because perhaps of one of the worst outbreak of this disease every experienced in that or any other country so far as I know. Let us keep that in mind. Is it not an indication that both Dr. Torrance and Dr. Mohler were careful, cautious and well-informed officials of their respective governments? Now, up to this point we have nothing but what is of the highest, and most commendable character in regard to this official -who was so summarily discharged. The first clause I read is in these words:
It is quite possible, however, that a suggestion may be made that we should modify our quarantine-
Remember, Dr. Torrance is writing to Dr. Mohler. Now, this is the point:
There was an expectation that a request for modification of the quarantine regulations would be asked for by Great Britain.
Hon. members will note that the request is expected to be made by Great Britain. This is the crux of the whole business, and I am sure, will persuade hon. members that there is nothing in the contention of the minister.
-so as to reduce the time of detention, and it is with regard to this possible demand that I would like to have confidentially your (Dr. Mohler's) opinion as it affects the relations between the Bureau and the Health of Animals branch.
That is, between the third country, the United States, and Canada. Now I come to the paragraph which is so offensive to the minister. Dr. Torrance continues.
I am strongly of the opinion that quarantine regulations should be based upon scientific knowledge.
Supply-Agriculture

Is there any objection to that? Is that sound, or is it offensive? Is it right or is it wrong? Is Dr. Torrance on good ground, or is he flirting with some influence that is injurious to this government? These are the questions that the committee are called upon to decide. He continues:
I am strongly of the opinion that quarantine regulations should be based upon scientific knowledge of the diseases against which we desire protection, of the conditions surrounding the traffic in animals, the freedom from disease of the country from which the cattb* are exported, and the time occupied in ocean travel.
These, he said, are the considerations that should be borne in mind; these are the influences that should determine the nature of the regulations to be passed. Now we get to the offence. I ask the minister,

and I wish the Prime Minister were in his seat, because this is an important matter, and it affects the government-and I ask the committee, to listen to this point, keeping in mind what I said a moment ago, that it,was anticipated that pressure would be brought to bear upon the Canadian	authorities-Dr.

Except his dismissal.

And, if you ask
me, I am sure that if Dr. Torrance's feelings were consulted in this matter he would request to be saved from his friends.
I think he would, seeing that the minister has included himself among his friends.

I do not see the
point. However, let me continue with the letter. Evidently, Mr. Chairman, hon. gentlemen do not like the corroborative evidence.
We have not heard it yet.
Who does not?

Let us get back to the document itself. I say with all respect-that I have never seen an officer in any department, and certainly have never had anything to do with one, who would write a letter of that character, especially to a foreign government in whose files it would be kept. There is no question that all the members of the staff would know about it. And as a matter of fact, word came back to us that they were astonished at Washington that we should keep in our employ a man who would write such a letter.

Who said that? Will the minister tell us who is responsible for the statement that the officials in Washington had expressed astonishment at the fact that, as he puts it we should have kept such a man in our employ?

It came through
Dr. Mohler.
Very well; but who said it?

I understand it
came from Dr. Mohler.
Did Dr. Mohler say that he was astonished?
Yes.

Will the minister take
the responsibility for saying that Dr. Mohler so stated?
I could not do that as he did not tell me.

It would be an affront
to common sense to suggest anything of the kind.

In fact, I expressed my own astonishment and my astonishment was given visibility by my interview with Dr. Torrance on the subject. My hon. friend forgets apparently that Dr. Torrance writes this:
If political considerations are to be introduced into the consideration of the question of quarantine, etc.
What can that mean-" if political considerations are to be introduced?" Obviously it is a complaint against some government or the department of some government; there is no question about that. All that fine-spun theorising on the part of my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) is the sort of argument of which only a lawyer could be capable; only a lawyer could so split hairs and pare cheese-
That is an accusation I cannot allow to pass unchallenged, Mr. Chairman.
It was not intended as an accusation.
The minister charged me-

I never charged you with anything. I simply say that I defy any hon. member over there, or for that matter anywhere else in the House, who has not a legal mind, to split hairs the way the hon. gentleman has done.
I am not a lawyer.

That being the
case, then, I have to compliment the hori. gentleman, for he certainly betrays a lawyer's mind in his aptitude for analysis and his ability to twist things and make them appear what they are not. Now, let me quote again the sentence to which I was calling the attention of my right hon. friend :
If political considerations are to be introduced into the consideration of the question of quarantine, etc.
I ask hon. members again, what can that possibly mean?	[DOT]

Does the minister infer
from that sentence any suggestion that Dr. Torrance is insinuating a play of party politics?

Supply-Agriculture
If that is not his meaning, what then is it?

How in the name of
common sense could party politics have anything to do with the statement as quoted by the minister? *

That is precisely
what I wanted to understand from Dr. Torrance; I wanted to know why he introduced politics into the matter.
Surely the minister can perceive the true significance of the sentence.
The minister cannot interpret the sentence as my right hon friend does; the minister must be very dense.
I think he is.
Well, hon. gentlemen will have to decide just where the density is.

Does the minister want to suggest that political pressure does not exist all the time, quite properly, between this country and Great Britain and every other country in the world? And does not political pressure in that connection always mean-unless any one wishes to import party into the matter-that there exist certain necessities and exigencies of government because of the demands of the people? Could anything be more manifest than that? And that is precisely what Dr. Torrance had in mind. Nothing else makes common sense; and while the minister may possibly be unable to conceive of a letter written in terms of common sense, I do not know why he should attribute such a state of mind to any of the officials of the department. The importation of the party sense into the meaning of the adjective in this case is utterly absurd and ridiculous, and the interpretation which the minister puts upon the sentence is altogether false; and the fact that the doctor sent the letter at once to the minister would show that if nothing else would.

My hon. friend is
at liberty to put any construction he likes upon it.

Dr. Torrance never
thought of putting any construction on it.

What the doctor
said-
I wonder who put that in his head.

Will the minister tell us
what he said?
142i

He wrote:
If political considerations are to be introduced into the consideration of the question of quarantine, it places the scientific advisers of the respective governments in a very anomalous position, and I feel that where we have to undertake the responsibility of carrying out any regulations that are made we should also have a decided influence in the planning of these regulations.
That was a straight intimation to me, who knew the circumstances; that it was penned because he did not have an opportunity of going over with the experts.

Did the minister charge
Dr. Torrance with the political partisanship that has just been referred to?

Dr. Torrance was
a political partisan of the first water.

That is not my question.
Did the minister discuss that aspect of the question with him?
No I do not think I did.

Did the minister have a
discussion with him at the time of his resignation?
That was the only discussion I had with him.
When was that?

About the first
week in July.	.
The 7th of July?
Yes. [DOT]
Did the minister have this letter from Dr. Mohler in reply of the 3rd November, 1922?

I do not know
whether I had or not, I have not the letter here. The 3rd November is a month afterwards. It would be about that, the reply came inside a month.
It is five days after.

That is inside a
month.

Has the minister that
letter?
Not here.
May I read a copy?

Do you mean from Dr. Mohler? Certainly. It has been read once already.
Supply-Agriculture

Did not the minister five
days after, receive the letter of Dr. Mohler and a copy of Dr. Torrance's letter to him?
I think so. We have Dr. Mohler's letter on file. I have read it. But as he is not responsible to this House I did not bring a copy of his letter.

When did the minister
ever ask Dr. Torrance about this political partisanship?
I have no recollection of discussing it with him at all until the July following.
Did not the minister have the letters there?
Yes, but the session came on in January. Departmental business accumulates and is attended to when the session is over.

Will the minister tell us
the nature of the conversation at the time Dr. Torrance was dismissed?

Yes. I have already done so. I produced this letter and asked him to give an explanation of what he meant, who was bringing political pressure upon him to do so and so. His explanation was that it was not the Canadian government nor myself that he had in mind, but that the political pressure was being brought by the British government.
Wasn't it?

No, but reverting
to my previous remarks, apparently for reasons that led Dr. Mohler to say:	If you
are compelled to do so and so in connection with these regulations, then we will have to do so and so. There is no question Dr. Mohler's answer was prompted by the nature of Dr. Torrance's letter.

Has there been at any
time pressure from the British government to reduce the period of quarantine?
It has been discussed in connection with breeding cattle, but there has been nothing of what we usually term political pressure; there was a conference.

What kind of pressure
would the minister call it?

Just simply friendly negotiations. When you use the term political pressure, it is always capable of being understood as party politics.
[Mr. Motherwell.!	.

Has the minister the
correspondence in that matter with the British government?
I understand from my deputy that the correspondence is in connection with the lifting of the embargo and is marked confidential.

The minister could not
lay it on the Table of the House?

We will look it
over. I think we took the file off last year and laid it on the Table with the Prime Minister's correspondence.
On July 7, when the conversation took place, did the minister demand Dr. Torrance's resignation?

After I showed
him this letter I told him I thought the time had come for us to dissolve partnership.
Did Dr. Torrance ask for an 'opporunity to consult his friends?

No and yes. He
asked for an opportunity to see Premier King.
Did he ask for time to reflect upon it?

He asked for an
opportunity to see Premier King. I told him that I had already seen the Premier.

You would not let the
Doctor see the Premisr.

Did he ask for time to
consider his position?

I do not recall
whether he did or not. He asked for an opportunity to see the Premier.

Was the question of his
gratuity or allowance discussed?
Surely.

Were any arrangements
made?

We started right
there to discuss it when he asked for an opportunity to see Premier King. I said I had already seen the Premier and my colleagues with respect to the matter. When he found that out he began discussing the retiring regulations and the amounts.

What was the nature of
the discussion?

Supply-Agriculture

Along the lines of
his length of service and the computation based upon it. I remember there were a number of years when he was engaged intermittently in Winnipeg, and there was some doubt whether those would count.
Was any amount discussed?

We discussed the
length'of time, and my memory is that his total service, including the period in doubt, was seventeen years, and excluding this period it was ten or eleven years of continuous employment. He was employed by the government intermittently in Winnipeg as inspector for about six years. He raised the question if I did not think that under the circumstances, he was within a year of being entitled to retire-he was sixty-four years of age-and would I consider a proposal to count the whole period. I do not know what the terms were. I said I would put a favourable interpretation on his claim to be considered as having been in the service seventeen years. We did so. It went through the usual routine -I can never remember all the different rigamaroles that have to be gone through- but that computation was refused by the Auditor General.

The minister is now getting away from the point. I am referring to the discussion about the specific amount that Dr. Torrance would receive if he resigned instead of being dismissed. What was the amount mentioned to him?

I have told my
hon. friend.
No, you have not mentioned the amount at all.

I cannot remember all these things. I do remember the period of years because it came up two or three times later. It does not make any difference what the amount was. We put the most favourable construction on the time, and called it seventeen years.
That is not the point.
I do not know.

I am asking a specific
question respecting a specific conversation and a specific fact mentioned in that conversation. Did the minister represent to Dr. Torrance that if he resigned the specific amount would be $1,500?
If those in authority over me, that is the Auditor General or the Audit Board-my hon. friend must remember that I am not the court of last appeal-
That is not my question.

Yes, we discussed
it, and so far as I am concerned, I was going to favourably consider the longest period that he suggested, seventeen years.
That is not an answer yet.

I do not know
the amount. How could I remember it?
Did not the minister mention $1,500?
I do not know today how the time is computed.
That is not the point. Did not the minister tell Dr. Torrance that if he resigned instead of being dismissed he would get an allowance of $1,500?
On the face of it that could not be so.

That is not the question.
Did the minister tell Dr. Torrance that he would get an allowance of $1,500.
No.
That is the answer.

How could I tell
him that? I did not tell him anything specific, because the matter was in doubt. But I did tell him he would get the most favourable consideration that I could give him, based upon the long period that he suggested- seventeen years. It went through the usual formula until it got to the Auditor General, and the Auditor General would not let the last six years count. Then he came back to me and we had negotiations with the Civil Service Commission. I had correspondence with Dr. Torrance; he wrote to me about it too, indicating that the amount that he was being allowed was less than he had anticipated. I wrote back and said I had recommended the amount that he wanted, but that the Auditor General would not let it go through. I presume that is one of the reasons the Auditor General is there-to check up anything that exceeds the exact regulations and to see that these things are subjected to the proper interpretation, which a great many of us cannot be expected always to have at our fingers' ends.

Before the clock strikes six, may I make a suggestion? There were a number of letters that the minister did not have on the file. I presume that this matter will go on this evening, and I suggest that he bring the remainder of the file with him.
C.N-R.-Branch Lines

The hon. gentleman means the letter from Dr. Mohler and the correspondence with Dr. Torrance? I shall be pleased to produce those.
Mr. MEIGHE'N: And particularly produce the evidence that Dr. Mohler expressed the opinion that we should not retain an official who would write that letter.
Oh, he would not put that on file.

No, I do not think he
would put it on file or on his lips or anywhere else, and never did.
Oh, yes.
It is merely a pipe dream on the part of the minister.

I will venture the guess that there was not an officer in Washington in the department concerned by whom this was not a subject of conversation, and just of the nature I have suggested.	.

subtopic: BILLS PROPOSED TO AUTHORIZE THE CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINES

speechtext:
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the House go into committee to consider Bill 31, respecting construction of a Canadian National Railway line between Grande Fresniere and Rinfret Junction.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

Suggestions were made in committee by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) and by the hon. member for St.. John (Mr. Baxter). The amended bill provides that the average mileage of each line and the cost per mile shall be stated. In one bill there was a suggestion that a fuller statement than we had proposed in the original bill as to expenditure and so on shall be provided and placed on the Table of the House each year. An amendment was proposed by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter) that the construction of the line should not begin if, after final estimates had been given by the engineers, they were of the opinion that the line would cost more than the amount stated in the bill. I think these were the three things.
On section 1-Power to construct and complete line described in schedule._

This is a branch
line connecting with the Huberdeau line.
Yes.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Company may issue securities and Governor in Council may authorize guarantee thereof.'

We are not objecting to the line. It is a proper one to be built. But we will have to adhere to the principle we invoked last year, that the amount to be guaranteed to any Canadian National line shall be shown in the estimates, as has already been done in reference to past construction. The bill as it stands does not require that. I therefore, move that the following proviso, which gives the right to the

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
government to guarantee, shall be added to this section:
Provided the amount so to be guaranteed shall first be included in the Estimates and voted by parliament for that purpose.
This was thoroughly debated last session, and there is nothing new in it. Our position still is that parliament should be in control of all matters of capital expenditure year by year, and we contend that the control of parliament is lost if the bill is put through in this form. The other point that we think of great importance is that unless the amounts so to be spent are included in the annual budget of the railways submitted to the House there is no proper basis of comparison, and we are changing in a very vital manner our past practices, thus forbidding anything like a proper comparison. For those reasons, which were urged at great length last session, I move this amendment.

This matter, as my hon.
friend says, was very thoroughly discussed last year and parliament decided that the three-year programme, as we have outlined it, is the more practical way of constructs ing these lines. There is a precedent in the way, not of a guarantee, but of a straight vote of cash, in which the item did not appear at all at any time in the Estimates. That is the grant to highways. There are many other statutory payments as regards which the items appear in the Estimates only as a matter of record and guidance noted as "paid by statute." and are not voted year after year.
What are those?

Technical Education,
Employment Service of Canada, Aid to Agriculture and the Highways Grant did not appear in the Estimates at any time. I speak having some knowledge because the highways were in the same department over which I am now presiding, and I know the reasons which actuated the government then in not putting those items into the Estimates. If those items were placed in the regular Estimates each year, they would be confined to a certain expenditure. The amount to be expended each year on highways depended altogether upon the amount that the provinces to which this grant was given would expend; but nevertheless, this expenditure was, to a certain extent, under the control of the Department of Railways and Canals, because no money could be paid out of the consolidated revenue of Canada except on the report of the engineers of the Department of Railways and Canals and the approval of the plans and of the construction as well. It was practical to
do this in that way, although it was somewhat of a departure. This is practical, and I submit that even if there were no precedent, it is time that we had one. Take the construction of branch lines scattered throughout the Dominion of Canada. If you have a vote each year, there is a constant fear of interference with construction, because each year the estimates have to be voted. To-day we find ourselves asking for authority to construct these lines, but they cannot be commenced before these bills pass through this House, go through the Senate and are signed by the Governor General and approved. If there were estimates, the case would be just the same. The estimates are not before the House yet, and we would be dragging along with our estimates until June or, perhaps, later. In this way, while no control is taken away from parliament, because provision is made in the bill that every expenditure and proposed expenditure must be placed on the table of the House each year for discussion by parliament, action can be taken on this construction each year. But there is this great advantage, that construction is continuous until the expiration of the act. Next year, say during the winter, on account of this act being in force for three years, the companies who have charge of this construction can get out their ties without any fear of having their railway construction stopped on account of the estimates. They can proceed with their construction on the very first day that the season of construction opens. Consequently, before harvest Itime comes;, when so many men are wanted, particularly in the West, 'they will have a great deal of construction done. I will give a concrete example. In 1920, if I remember correctly, one-half approximately of the branch lines that we are now asking for power to complete were started under an estimate. Had there been a three-year programme, one-half of *he lines which we are now asking for power to construct, would have been constructed and the trains running over them; but no estimate was asked for in a later year and the construction stopped. The only practical way to work out this construction is on the basis of a three-year programme, with full particulars of everything done and proposed to be done to be laid on the table each year for the consideration of members.

I have heard the minister's argument on this point several times, and I have no doubt that he has heard me express my contentions several times. Nevertheless, I purpose repeating them, because, needless to say, I have not in the slightest
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

degree altered my view, and it becomes more and more firm every time I hear the minister express his views. The minister says: The reason we do not want to come to parliament for this appropriation each year is, first, that there are precedents in respect of other legislation where a several years' programme was provided and where the money did not require to be voted to be spent each year. He cites some at my request. I will deal with this argument first. There is no precedent in connection with the National Railways. From the very commencement of that enterprise, every dollar from the beginning to the end of the year each year was voted' by parliament, whether it was to be raised by way of specific loan to the enterprise or by way of guarantee, and it is of some importance that the books of this country present a sequence; that we do not keep turning and twisting our method of bookkeeping and thereby confusing the whole electorate and taxpayers of Canada. This is what we are doing in more spheres than one now. But there is no precedent, not only in the National Railways, but in anything else, save based on a definite principle, and that principle sticks out from every case cited by the minister. What were the cases he mentioned? He mentioned the Technical Education Act, the Agricultural Instruction Act, the Employment Service of Canada and the Highways Act. Those were the four. I do not think there are any more. The minister knows just as well as I the great difference in that class of cases from the ordinary case. What is the difference? Why, there we were passing legislation for co-operative work with other governments. The other governments had to have, the basis of a statutory enactment. They had to know whether they would enter into this construction extended over a period of years with the government of Canada. They wanted to know what they could depend upon. This was, in a word, not something wholly within the compass of this parliament; it was something that depended upon the will of another body over which we had no control at all, which was not our creation, a distinct and separate government. That applies to the whole of them. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) will remember all this because he was in the government then.

I have just come in and
I did not catch the first part of my right hon. friend's remarks.

I am calling attention to the distinction of the cases where we have

passed legislation providing for statutory annual payment up to a definite maximum each year, without the necessity of coming every year to parliament for a vote. The cases cited by the minister were Technical Education, Agricultural Instruction, Highways and Employment Service. Each and every one of them was a case in which there was cooperation with other governments who contributed their share. I know of no other case.
The minister said that we are going to establish a precedent now if we never had one before. I submit that in the first place this utterly destroys the sequence of our bookkeeping; and if the minister is going to take this course, then for goodness' sake let him put a curb on the tongue of his Prime Minister or some of the other ministers, maybe his own, instead of continually coming to the House and saying, "Just look at the estimates; see how much less they are than those of last year. Behold the economists now in power!" For the sake of presenting intelligently to the people of Canada the real state and currency of public affairs, do not let us keep changing our methods of bookkeeping. If we are bound to do so we shall; but we certainly do not have to in the present instance. "But," says the ministeV, "we have to get out ties and we want to know whether or not we shall be able to go on. We are building so many miles this year and we want to know just what we shall be able to do in this direction next year." Well, have we never built lines before? What is the obstacle now? The minister knows that the government of which he was a member, when it built the National Transcontinental, came to parliament every year for the money that was required; and I never read in Hansard in those days, nor did I hear while I was in the House, any complaint from the minister or any suggestion that there was a handicap in the government's having to do this. The minister objects that he has to wait for the vote. How long is he obliged to wait? No sooner has parliament met than the government can secure an appropriation; they can get one-sixth right away. There is absolutely nothing in the world . to hinder them from doing this any year. The minister must realize that it is all a humbug to talk about having to wait until parliament votes the money. There has been no difficulty at all in getting preliminary estimates passed. Why not accept the amendment? I should like a suggestion from the minister before I sit down. I am quite sure that he would not be hampered in the slightest if he accepted the system suggested, and it would preserve the sequence qf the methods of bookkeeping

C.N-R.-Branch Lines
and enable the public really to judge of the comparisons of one year with another.
The minister said that we had control anyway. My contention is that we have no control, and I should have pointed that fact out before. We have no more control after we have committed ourselves. It is true we could repeal the act; but we could also repeal the Agricultural Instruction Act or any similar act. But that would not be the right thing to do in the case where we have a contract with other governments; it would not be honourable. The minister argues that we have control even though we may not vote the money every year, because parliament must be told each year what is. to be done, so that parliament can complain and grouse about it if it wants to. That is true. But what is the use of doing that when parliament has no check? And then the next breath the minister says that if in 1920 the late government had adopted the course which is now proposed, instead of the course it then took, the roads would have been built. What does that mean? It means that if we had put a bill through and tied the hands of parliament, whether or not we felt we could afford to go on from year to year, we would have had the work done. Is that consistent with the minister's contention that parliament has control? The fact is that in that case parliament would have no control. So that we are taking out of the hands of parliament its primary function in the control of annual expenditure. That is the first duty of the House, and if we are going to establish this precedent now where shall we end? We could advance in respect to any mortal thing just the argument that the minister is making to-night. For instance, in the construction of this building, the minister of that day could have stood up and said:	"We do not want
to have to come to parliament every year because we may find ourselves, With the foundations laid, unable to proceed, and parliament might refuse to vote the money. The contractor wants to know whether he will be able to go on next year and the year after that and for that reason we do not want to be under the necessity of coming to parliament every year." That is exactly the * argument which the minister is presenting at the present time; and I say that if we adopt any such course the temptation to every government will be to do the same thing and we should be in a hopeless mixup and the public in a worse.

The matter was so
thoroughly discussed last year, when it was approved of by parliament, that I do not
intend taking up the time of the committee at any great length to-night. I outlined in committee the method of financing the undertaking but it was not discussed; and while I fully expected my right hon. friend to raise the point he has brought up, I really do not think that there is anything in it. I am not speaking with any intention of being discourteous. Parliament has just as much control in the matter as it has ever had, for a full statement is given to the House every year. My right hon. friend suggested that we could repeal other acts, such as the Highways Act, but that inasmuch as they involved co-operation with provinces it would not be honest to do that. In other words, if such an act had no reference to any province it would be all right to repeal it. Now, if it were found that there was something radically wrong there is no question that any of these bills could be repealed as easily as an estimate can be dropped. But for practical purposes I submit again that the method we propose is the most advisable, under present labour conditions and the conditions generally in the country which are of a character that did not prevail at all when the Transcontinental was constructed. The conditions in relation to the Transcontinental were different from those under which the work in this case is being done, because labour was especially provided for in the case of the Transcontinental, whereas in connection with these branch lines the labour that is available in the particular district will be utilised, it is expected, without interfering unduly with the farmers' help in the busy season. Parliament undoubtedly has full control in the matter, but this I say is the practical way of doing it. The government, the railway board and the engineers are of the opinion that the lines could be built fairly expeditiously and at a .minimum cost, and there is nothing to hide nor is there any intention of hiding anything.

How does the minister
distinguish these branch lines from the hundreds of branch lines that have been built before?

The minister is constructing the Welland canal, but he does not take in respect of that work, the position he' holds now. He lets a contract in that case, to run, say, three or four years, but each year he comes to parliament with [DOT] his estimates so that parliament can decide what money shall be spent in any particular year. This is all we ask in respect of these railways.
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The controversy seems to be as to whether we shall vote a definite sum for a period of three years if the bill is passed.
We do not vote anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Each one of these lines calls for a fixed sum.

We are voting
nothing; this is not a voting bill. The bill is to get away from that. The whole question is whether we are to vote funds or not.

The mind of my hon.
friend (Mr. Stewart) is in the right state, and I hope he will not have it affected by contact with his colleague the Minister of Railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My understanding was that there was to be a fixed sum in each of the bills.
But we are not getting a chance to vote it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Is it not in the bill?
We are asked to pass the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think there is a fixed sum attached to each bill and beyond that the railway board cannot go unless they secure a further sum for the purposes for which it is required. My hon. friend says that annually we should put that sum in the estimates of the proposed amount to be spent that year. If that is done, each year the contractor or the board will have to await the vote before they make their arrangements to carry on the work, which undoubtedly means, as my hon. friend knows perfectly well, that it will be at least June before construction work is started, quite apart from the purchase of ties.

Was it June in the case of the National Transcontinental? Was it June in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific? Was it June in the case of the branch lines that are already mostly built? In respect of every one of these there was a vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Both my hon. friend and I are familiar with the railway 'guaranties given by both the federal and provincial governments. For example, $20,000 a mile was guaranteed on a certain mileage of road. Parliament voted it and the government were given authority to pay it out on progress estimates. My recollection is that we did not vote the money annually by way of estimates.
We voted every dollar.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have a
perfectly clear recollection of the provincial procedure. I merely mention it in passing as the method by which construction was carried on. There was no cessation of construction; it went on continuously until the amount voted by parliament for the specific purpose was exhausted. Now you have here a three-year contract. I have no particular desire to withhold anything from parliament, but my understanding is that we are voting for each one of these lines a certain specific sum of money-if I a,m wrong I should like to be . corrected-and that it is to be spent over a period of three years. If that is the case, I fail to see that parliament has not full control of the amount voted specifically for each line. If that amount is exhausted, certainly parliament will be called upon to vote more money. If we were not voting this specific amount I am not sure that there would not be a good deal in the contention of my hon. friend, but under the circumstances I cannot see why we have not complete control.
Why would not everything the minister says apply to the Welland canal or any other public work?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
know the conditions surrounding the Welland canal. My argument is that you are voting, for example, $2,000,000 by the enactment of this bill, and you are consulting parliament norw as to the amount that will be expended upon each one of these branch lines.
Why should this parliament decide wihat the next parliament may do?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There may be something in that contention. But my hon. friend is arguing that parliament has no control over the expenditure. I contend that parliament has absolute control under this bill.

I argue that parliament
has no control year by year as it ought to have over all expenditure year by year. Think of a Liberal government, boasting its liberalism standing here between parliament and its rights in a case which is not distinguishable in any degree from any public works that have been undertaken for the past fifty years I

I am not going to follow my right hon. friend, because I have stated the case from the pure business standpoint, and my friend the Minister of the Interior

C.NJt.-Branch Lines
has supported my argument. I am not sure after all that it would not save this country money if in every public work the full amount of the expenditure was put in at the start, either in the bill or otherwise.
Does the minister favour that?

My hon. friend as a
member of former governments has consented to start a work costing $200,000 on a $20,000 estimate. Unless a member has had experience he will imagine he is voting for a $20,000 expenditure, and in the absence of a full explanation he will be surprised when year after year the vote eventually runs up to $200,000. Now, we are inserting in these bills the full cost of construction, and a clause, suggested by the hon.. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter) has been added that if the engineers find after final surveys that the work is likely to cost more than this amount, construction is not to be started until after we have come back to parliament. That is pretty good control.
Has not that control always existed?
No.
Of course it has in every other case.

The clause suggested is
not in any other bill that I know of.

Certainly it is not, because in the other cases the money is voted year by year; why in the world would it be inserted there? How does he think the country is going to save any money merely because it is stated in the bill in the first place what the total cost is to be? If it turns out that the cost is more, you just come back to parliament and get the extra money; that is all.

My hon. friend does not catch the point. Before the company start this work if they find out it is going to cost more than the amount stated they have to come back to parliament before they spend any money on construction at all; while with the usual estimate, after you have spent $10,000 or $20,000 you cannot stop even if in the long run the total cost exceeds $200,000.

Suppose the engineers
turn out to be wrong in their estimate?

There is a possibility of that always, but we have to depend on human agencies. In the estimate, I suggest the engineers know when they start that the work
will cost $200,000, but only $20,000 is asked in the estimate, and those of us not in touch with the situation would be committing the country for $200,000 when we thought we were only committing it for $20,000. In this case every member knows exactly the amount intended to be expended on each branch line. Let me point out that I am informed that in the United States all large contracts for public works are voted for a term of years with the entire amount expected to be expended contained1 in the first vote. They have to report progress to congress each year with full information of what has been done: but until the amount voted in the first estimate is exhausted congress is not asked for any further vote.	That is the
principle of this bill.
Suppose a work is to cost $10,000,000, and to be built over a period of ten years, is the whole $10,000,000 charged in the estimate of the one year in the comparison of that year with another?
I do not know how the bookkeeping works out, but I do know they state the whole amount in the estimate for the entire work; at least full information is given as to the entire work.

Certainly; and in this
parliament too.
There is nothing new in this, it is a purely business proposition. It was the same in respect to our highways, where parliament had power to step in any year.

As I understand the minister, certainly the legislative body gets full information. And we ought to get every time all the best information the engineer can give of what the total expenditure will be. But to suggest, that the United States Senate and House of Representatives vote one year the money that is to be expended over a long period of years in great enterprises- why, does the minister suggest that the cost of the Panama canal was voted in one year?
I do not know what legislation was in force then.
There would be no continuity in the estimate at. all then. Do what is done in the United States; that will be satisfactory to us.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We are voting for this particular line, $357,000, and we are asking that construction may be over a period of three years. The amount may be expended in two years if the work is carried

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
on successfully. I confess I have no particular objection to what my hon. friend says, except this: You will run the construction to a late period in the summer if you have to wait annually for estimates for construction. If you vote $20,000 for this line this year and you spend the whole of that amount, no further work can be done until a new vote is taken after the 31st of March next.
What is the trouble about getting a new vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
suppose there would be any trouble, if parliament decides that this line shall be built. But you do stop the continuity of construction.
In what way?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Any railway construction in this country must be carried on before frost sets in, and if you have to wait for an estimate the next year, with a short season for railway construction, you will be into June before you can begin work again. Labour is a movable commodity in Canada; railwaymen desert railway work in the harvest season, particularly in the West, and that means that the cost of railway construction is added to. I would be the last to argue that any right should be taken from parliament or that parliament should not know exactly what is being done with the money voted. But when you vote this $357,000 for 12 miles of railway, there is absolute control under the provisions of the present bill, and you have a period of three years within which to spend the money if that length of time is required for the construction.

I do not like to see my hon. friend do so much violence to his principles. He does not want to take away parliamentary control. Well, he does not have to do it; he can stay by his principles if he wants to. In the first place, we are not voting money by this bill; we are simply enabling the government to exercise certain rights of guarantee. I am sure my hon. friend will be horrified to find that a single cent should be spent unless it is properly voted by parliament, but as I say we are not by this legislation voting a dollar. My hon. friend knows how votes are made effective. He knows about the Supply Bill; he knows about the statutory estimates. He knows that our supply bills are charges upon our consolidated revenue fund. He knows all about our system of bookkeeping, and checks here and checks there, i He knows how these systems are used for the purposes of comparison in arriving at an idea of the value of ser-

vices here and services there. These are the principles my hon. friend stands for, but they all go, so far as these lines are concerned. It is idle to talk about a three-year period within which construction may be completed. There is no reason why this little line should not be built at once, particularly in the prairies where no difficulties in construction are encountered, and the way to get these lines built at once is to have the votes appear in the year's estimates. My hon. friend is right in saying that railway construction work cannot proceed when the frost is in the ground, and that there is only a short season. But every autumn and winter the preparations can be made, material, ties and all that sort of thing got ready, for the commencement pf work as soon as the frost is out of the ground. That is what always has been done under the annual vote. My hon. friend knows, too, that the vote is carried over for six weeks after the statutory year, and also that as a matter of course interim supply is voted. Looking at it in the light of his own principles, which he has already enunciated, my hon. friend, it seems to me, will have to vote against this proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am sure
my hon. friend does not want to misquote me. I do not see that I am violating any principle. I understand perfectly well that the company may issue bonds,
9 p.m. notes, or securities which the government may guarantee for the construction of these lines. My hon. friend says that these lines ought to be built in one year. I do not know whether that could be done, but it is obvious that there can be no guarantee beyond the amount specified in the act, and if you were voting the money direct the same principle would apply. As I understand it, my hon. friend is not objecting to the amount, $357,000; he simply says that such portion of that amount should be voted each year as may be required for that year.

My hon. friend
has not quite got the point If there is to be any real consistency in the carrying on of the public business these items ought to appear in the estimates this year and just the same for the one' year as for the three years.
