On section 4.-Mileage and1 cost are estimates only but not to be exceeded by more than 15 per cent.

In view of the fact that
clause 5 is now incorporated in the bill-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We have not got to
clause 5 yet, we are considering clause 4.

I wish to discuss clause
4 in the light of clause 5. I should like to ask the minister if 15 per cent is not rather small. As I understand clause 5, it means that should a re-survey of a branch line that has been already started disclose the cost to be more than 15 per cent above the amount named in the bill, the work will not be undertaken. In view of the fact that the cost of labour and of material fluctuates, and delay in construction work is sometimes caused by bad weather, a 15 per cent margin is very small. That would mean that many of the branch lines might not be built this year. If that is the case the situation is rather serious because many families in some of these districts are simply holding on believing they are going to have these branch lines this year. Should the lines not be built they intend to move out. I may be wrong in my interpretation of this clause and if so I should like to be set right.

There may be something
in what my hon. friend says. This provision of 15 per cent was placed in the bill to meet an objection which had been raised that the minister had too much authority and could go on under the old bill and spend all that he desired, as his estimates as to distance and cost were only approximate. I think the interpretation my hon. friend has drawn is all right, and being of that opinion I am inclined to believe it is not a bad idea to hold the engineers to the estimate. In the case of lines partially constructed they ought to be able to estimate pretty carefully, because in a good many instances all they are going to do is to lay the steel. It may be a small percentage as my hon. friend says, but the engineer assured me the other day in discussing this matter we were safe in fixing that amount in any of the estimates particularly in the case of those lines in which there had been partial construction.

I think that so far as the prairie lines are concerned there ought not to be the slightest difficulty, unless a sink hole is encountered or some unforeseen trouble. But I anticipate the only place where there may be trouble is where an expensive piece of bridge work has to be done or some extraordinary bit of country encountered. In the case of prairie lines I should think there would be absolutely nothing of the kind. The whole proposition was as to whether there was to be an absolutely free hand given without the slightest control. I do not think my hon. friend need worry about the way the section reads.

There might be difficulty where rock was unexpectedly struck or something of that kind, or where deep cuts were needed, but provision for that would be made in the final estimates. In the construction of prairie lines I do not think there will be any difficulty.

I think the limit is quite adequate. If the engineers have .made a careful survey of the line they ought to be able to tell within 15 per cent of what the estimated cost would be. If rock should be struck, where there has been partial construction, as the minister suggested, and the amount is insufficient, the matter could be rectified the following year.

But if construction was to take place this year, and by chance 15 per cent was not sufficient to complete the line to, say, within one mile of its terminal, that would be a very serious difficulty, and very great hardship might result. I am inclined to take the same view as my hon. friend (Mr. Millar).

Section agreed to.

I want to make just a little explanation while this bill is going through. When this matter was in the resolution stage,
I spoke on behalf of this line being connected up with Swift Current, and the Swift Current paper made a comment on the situation that the bill was not. providing a railway running into Swift Current. speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would like the word "southeasterly" in the title amended to read "easterly." The Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National had some controversy about the line running south of the Saskatchewan. That, I understand, has been adjusted and the line will go in so as to give service to the people along the river. It is suggested that the one line would serve that north country by its diversion to the north. However, the engineers have been asked to make a reconnaissance of that country to see whether by going a little further north with this extension easterly from St. Paul they could give the needed service, when the line is built in between the Canadian National and the river, to the south.

This does not make any
material change, does it, in the direction and location indicated to the committee on the maps when we were examining into the matter? If it does, of course we ought to scrutinize it with a little more care.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the line
runs in a southeasterly direction from St. Paul de Metis it certainly will not be of any

service to Bonnyville and the thickly settled territory to the north of St. Paul. These settlers requested that another line be built 10 or 15 miles to the westward of St. Paul, which would mean two lines1 in that locality. By this line running a little more to the northward it might serve the locality much better and would still connect 10 p.m. with the line coming in from the eastward.
There is no material alteration in the general direction of this line?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
Is it the intention to use the present survey, or will there be an entirely new survey?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They would have to change the survey for this line, because it connects most directly between a point in Saskatchewan and St. Paul de Metis in Alberta.

I questioned the engineer very definitely on that point in the committee and he said they were going to use the same survey. I also asked about that other proposed branch:	The request is that
that line branch out at Ashmount and go up to the Cold Lake country, and he said it was one of the branches that 'they anticipated building some time, but not immediately. I tried to get him to make a commitment in the matter, because the provincial government are also considering building branches into that same territory.
The hon. member refers to what we described in the committee as the northerly route?

Yes. I thought it fair to the provincial government that the engineer should at least definitely state whether there was any prospect of their changing the route of this proposed branch and going farther north, and he said that was not expected at all, they were going to make use of the existing data.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am going to ask that we be given the opportunity, unless it is impossible, to serve these people; it is possible to go closer to them than is contemplated by the proposed line. It is a very difficult thing to interfere with the engineers. We will have to abide by their decision after all.

It is my opinion that the country about which we are talking is so large that it cannot be served by one railway.

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
I think that a line will have to go somewhere along the proposed route. Perhaps it may go a little north but of course that will have to be left to the engineers. There will have to be another line running farther north probably starting from Ashmont and serving the country of St. Vincent, Rife, Bonnyville, Durlingville and tapping the Cold Lake country. I think this will be necessary because the country north of the Beaver river is a good country, and just as soon as there is railway transportation within reasonable distance there is not the slightest doubt in my mind but that it will be settled. The Minister of the Interior mentioned that there was a line going from Lloydminister in a northwesterly direction between the river and the present Canadian National line, and he intimated that this would serve those people as far as the river, possibly those just the other side of the river. I think that was his intention. It is pretty difficult without having a map before us to get hon. members to realize the huge distances that have to be traversed in that part of the country. For instance the distance from Vermilion to the river, Saskatchewan, is about forty-seven miles. Now if you split that country with a railway, as it is the intention to do, even then there are twenty-three odd miles before you get to the river. Then there are the very steep banks of the Saskatchewan river to be crossed before you reach the other side. Therefore I do not think that railway will be of very much service to the people on the other side of the Saskatchewan. Of course it would have to be left to the judgment of the engineers, but in my opinion if we are going to keep the people who are already settled in that country in great numbers-having gone in on the promise of a railway years ago-two railways will have to be constructed to serve that huge territory. Of course we realize that we cannot get all these facilities at once, but I do hope that the railway suggested in this bill will be started this year. I have had letters this last week from several people in that vicinity recounting the number of settlers who were losing heart and pulling out. They have been there for many years, and they hoped every year to see the railway come along. Up to the present time it has not come, and they now hear rumours that the route may be changed to this point or the other point. It is this very uncertainty that is losing us at the present time a number of settlers. I sincerely hope that if this bill goes through, as I hope it will, that it will Be started this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Am I to
understand my hon. friend does not want the amendment?

I have no objection to
the amendment as long as the railway is not taken too far north. It could go northeasterly or southeasterly, but if the route followed is easterly I do not think there will be much harm done.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is
agreeable to me.
But it is my opinion that we cannot serve that country properly with only one railway.

Regardless of what the
amendment provides there ought to be some information as to what particular township you expect to land up in when you get that twenty-one miles constructed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My proposition is to leave it entirely to the engineer.

If you do that, in the
event of the engineer being sincere in the statement to the committee, it will go right where the survey is now.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
help that. I may say for the information of the committee that I had representations from a delegation that came down here from Bonnyville at considerable expense. These people have been in the country for sixteen years. I am not sanguine that the engineers will change this route but what I did ask them to do was to make a reconnaissance of the country from Ashmont via Bonnyville to Cold lake. If the line were to run in an easterly direction it might not serve the Bonnyville territory because they would have to travel a considerable distance to the railway.

Is it your' opinion that
one railway will serve that country?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I would not
like to say.

I suppose the real object
of the amendment is to give the engineers a little more latitude rather than to tie them up to one location?
How does the amendment now read?

That the line shall be
easterly.

Instead of a southeasterly direction? Is that the only change?
C.N.R.-Branch Lines
That is the only change.
It is in some township.

There is no township
mentioned.

The schedule of the bill
reads:
From St. Paul in a southeasterly direction to a point in or near township 57, range 6, west of the 4th meridian, in the province of Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The title
reads now:
From St. Paul in the province of Alberta southeasterly twenty-one miles.

We are not concerned
about that. That is merely a title.

I should like to point
out that if this railway is going to end up in township 63 or 64 it will be an entirely different matter. You are getting the line away altogether from the settlement which is down along the Saskatchewan river.

Township 57, range 6, it
says in the schedule.
But if the road is run in an easterly direction it will probably end in township 63 or 64. The committee should have more information on the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the line
is going to end in section 57 there is no use in amending the bill. We might as well leave it alone. I do not think it is a mistake, however.

Do I understand the
minister aright that he considers the Elk Point country not as good as the Bonnyville country?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would say they are about similar.

I think they are very similar. I appreciate the position the Minister of the Interior is in, having had a delegation down here, but the trouble is that I have had representations from two sources, pulling in opposite directions.

Which direction do you
pull in?
The largest representation is asking for the railway along the line of the original survey, but I realize that another railway has to be built to serve the people further north.

I think the Minister
of the Interior has brought some of the trouble on his own head. I have a copy of a letter which appeared in the Edmonton Journal purporting to be from the Minister of [Mr. Stevens.2
the Interior to the Edmonton Board of Trade, and which reads:
I have been very busy securing an extension of this line from St. Paul de Metis eastward, and have succeeded in having an amount included in the branch lines bills. It does not necessarily follow that any particular location has to be adopted, and I am now prepared to discuss location with the delegation, and to press their views upon the engineers who will be in charge of the extension.
The Edmonton Journal comments on this letter as follows:
What the delegation is seeking is an extension of the St. Paul branch in a northeasterly direction toward Cold Lake, so that it may serve a better and more productive section of the country than if it were routed in a southeasterly direction along the Saskatchewan river, as originally planned.
I thought I would mention this matter because I am quite convinced that it would probably be a good idea to leave these branch lines to the judgment of the engineers; we are advised from time to time that there is no undue political influence used, and I would not say there was even political influence in this letter.

Pretty strong,
but perhaps not undue.
I.am willing to congratulate the minister on the careful wording of the letter. It is very carefully worded.

I would like to suggest,
in view of the precedent laid down this afternoon in the peremptory discharge of an old civil servant for political interference with scientific procedure in connection with one department, that the minister who has undoubtedly allowed politics to enter into this important matter, interfering with the decision and opinion of the engineers, should be summarily dismissed and asked .outright for his resignation. That would create harmony in keeping with the policy of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am delighted with the letter and glad to hear the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). I am sure my hon. friend has often sought to work in the interests of his constituents. These are not my constituents; but I am interested in all the people in Alberta, and in any delegation that comes here, and I certainly will continue to try to use my influence to meet what I think are legitimate requests. If there is any harm in that then I am guilty. The Edmonton Board of Trade were interested in the line, and knowing the country as I do, I saw no harm in bringing it to the attention of the engineers, which I did. I got no promise from the engineers that they would

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
change the route. I did get a promise that they would make a survey of the whole country and make up their minds as to which was the best location to serve the people up there.

Perhaps the
committee will excuse the minister if he promises not to do it again.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I will not
promise that.

Will the minister explain if this statement that he was instrumental in getting a grant for an extension for 21 miles east of St. Paul de Metis is correct or was that done under the ordinary methods of procedure?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no grant. It is just in the same position as any other extension.
The hon. minister does not get my point.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I got it a long while ago. I get your point very frequently. Your point is to try to discredit anything that the Minister of the Interior might do in the vicinity of Edmonton. Now just keep right at it, so far as I am concerned. I am interested in all the people in the different localities. These branch lines are being discussed; delegations are coming here; letters are being written, and out of courtesy to the people who write the letters I have to take an interest in these things. In a sense the Board of Trade of Edmonton did make a request at the instance of the people in that locality, and I certainly have no apology to make.

What authority has the minister to make a statement that I was trying in any way to embarrass him? I have never done so in this House. If the reading of the letter is the trouble, I do not think the Minister of the Interior should be bothered.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Do you
think the letter is material to anything that has transpired to-day?
I did not say it was.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Then what
is the object of bringing it up?

There is one thing the minister might explain. He said he was instrumental in having a bill brought in in reference to the branch lines we are now discussing. That is not the function of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If suggesting this is one of the matters for the consideration of the railway board of the Board of Management of the Canadian National Railways or of the Canadian Pacific Railway,-because I have gone to both on the same mission, pressing the claims of these localities-is a crime, I have been guilty. Further than that I have not gone.
Would1 the minister be kind enough to tell us how to get in touch with the board? How is it done?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Go to Montreal.
I do not think my hon. friend really knows. Will the minister not tell us how it was done.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I invariably see the chairman, Sir Henry Thornton.

Will my hon.
friend tell me two things: First, what the business on Monday will be and, second, at what time we shall meet to do business on Monday? I think civic summer time goes into effect on Saturday at midnight.

I think, following precedent, that we adhere to the time established in the municipality, the city of Ottawa. That

will be daylight saving time. Let everybody put his clock on an hour. The business on Monday will be the estimates of the Minister of Labour, after that the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and if we get through with those, I will try to take up railway bills again.
